pos: n. (Flavius Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus, c. 485–c. 585, Roman senator under the Gothic kings who in retirement founded the monastery of Vivarium and set monks to copying books)
etymology: Latin Cassiodorus, from a Syrian family settled in Bruttium; the name is probably Greek, Kassiodoros, gift of Cassius.
biblical_def: Cassiodorus served Theodoric the Ostrogoth and his successors as quaestor, consul and praetorian prefect, and when the Gothic kingdom fell he withdrew to his family estate in Calabria and founded Vivarium. There he did the thing for which the West should thank him: he made the copying of manuscripts a monastic duty. His Institutiones divides study into divine and human letters and directs the monk first to the Scriptures and then to the grammar, rhetoric and logic that serve them. He insisted on accurate texts, kept correctors at work, and wrote a long exposition of the Psalms of his own. The warrant is 2Ti 4:13, where the apostle in prison asks for “the books, but especially the parchments,” and Joh 5:39, where the Lord says of the Scriptures, “they are they which testify of me.” Nearly every classical and patristic text the Middle Ages possessed came down through scriptoria that followed his pattern. He is not a theologian of the first rank and his Psalm commentary leans hard on Augustine, but the man who makes it possible for others to read the Word has done a work the church cannot do without.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a manuscript as a book or paper written with the hand or pen, as distinguished from one printed.
webster_full: M'ANUSCRIPT, n. A book or paper written with the hand or pen; a writing of any kind, in distinction from what is printed.
M'ANUSCRIPT, a. Written with the hand; not printed.
2. To transcribe; to copy.
scriptures: Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments.
Psa 1:2
But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
corruption_summary: The monastic copyist is now praised for saving classical civilization and seldom credited with the end he actually served, which was that men should read the Scriptures.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard account makes Vivarium a rescue operation for Greek and Roman letters, with Scripture as one item in the inventory. Cassiodorus ordered it the other way. His Institutiones begins with the divine letters and admits the human arts as servants: grammar so the text may be parsed, rhetoric so it may be preached, logic so error may be answered. Reverse that order and you have the Renaissance academy, where Scripture becomes one ancient text among many and Ecc 12:12 comes true — “of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.”

The second and nearer corruption is the modern evangelical indifference to textual labour. Cassiodorus thought an inaccurate copy a sin against the Word and paid men to compare manuscripts. A church that holds verbal plenary inspiration and shrugs at the transmission of the text does not believe its own doctrine. The recovery is his premise: because “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” the words themselves are worth a lifetime of care, and the humblest corrector at a desk is doing the work of Joh 5:39.
roots_summary: Greek eraunao (G2045), to search; biblion (G975), a book; membrana (G3200), a parchment.

Greek biblion (G975) — a book, a scroll; 2 Timothy 4:13.
Greek membrana (G3200) — a parchment, vellum; 2 Timothy 4:13.
Hebrew hagah (H1897) — to meditate, to murmur over; Psalm 1:2.
Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction; Psalm 1:2.

“the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13) — the apostle's own request.
“in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Psa 1:2) — the monastic day at its best.

pos: n. (Isidore of Seville, c. 560–636, archbishop of Seville and compiler of the Etymologies, the encyclopedia that taught the Middle Ages what it knew)
etymology: Greek Isidoros, gift of Isis — a pagan name borne by a Christian bishop, as Phoebe and Apollos were in the apostolic church.
biblical_def: Isidore of Seville governed the Spanish church for more than thirty years and presided at the Fourth Council of Toledo. His great work is the Etymologiae, twenty books that gather what late antiquity knew of grammar, law, medicine, agriculture, war, the church and the world, and explain each thing by the derivation of its name. The method rests on a conviction drawn from Gen 2:19, that naming is not arbitrary: Adam “called every living creature, that was the name thereof,” and a word therefore carries the nature of the thing. For a thousand years the Etymologies was the reference book of the West, quoted more often than any text but the Vulgate. Isidore also laboured to bring the Visigothic kingdom from Arianism into the Nicene faith and to order its worship and discipline. He writes as a man persuaded of Pro 25:2, that “the honour of kings is to search out a matter,” and of Pro 1:5, that “a wise man will hear, and will increase learning.” His etymologies are frequently wrong, sometimes wildly; his labour of gathering was nonetheless one of the great acts of Christian stewardship over knowledge.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines etymology as that part of philology which explains the origin and derivation of words, with a view to ascertain their radical or primary signification.
webster_full: ETYMOL'OGY, n. That part of philology which explains the origin and derivation of words, with a view to ascertain their radical or primary signification.
2. That branch of grammar which comprehends the derivation and inflection of words.
scriptures: Pro 25:2
It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.
Pro 1:5
A wise man will hear, and will increase learning; and a man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels:
Col 2:3
In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
Gen 2:19

And out of the ground the LORD God formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air; and brought them unto Adam to see what he would call them: and whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof.
corruption_summary: Isidore's confidence that a word's derivation yields the thing's nature is a half-truth that becomes a method of error when it is not checked by the text.
corruption_paragraphs: The etymological method has a real foundation and a real limit. Gen 2:19 grounds language in God's gift to Adam, and this dictionary is itself built on the conviction that words carry freight. But Isidore pressed the principle past evidence, deriving meanings from chance resemblances of sound and then reasoning from the derivation as though it settled the matter. In theology that habit is dangerous: it is the root of the preacher's word-study that makes a Greek root say what the sentence does not. Usage governs meaning, and the derivation is a servant of exegesis, never its substitute.

The second corruption is one Isidore himself resisted but his successors did not: the treatment of his encyclopedia as an authority beside Scripture. For centuries a question was settled by what Isidore said, and the compiler became a father. Col 2:3 locates the treasures — “In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” — in Christ, not in a book about the world. The recovery is to use reference works as reference works, honouring Isidore's immense diligence while holding that no compilation binds the conscience and that only the Scriptures are the rule of faith.

Greek thesauros (G2344) — a treasure, a storehouse; Colossians 2:3.

“A wise man will hear, and will increase learning” (Pro 1:5) — his working rule.
“In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col 2:3) — the limit his readers forgot.

pos: n. (Caesarius of Arles, c. 470–542, bishop of Arles, plain preacher to the common people, who presided at the Second Council of Orange in 529)
etymology: Latin Caesarius, of Caesar; Arles is the Roman Arelate in Provence.
biblical_def: Caesarius of Arles was trained at the island monastery of Lérins, made bishop of Arles about 502, and spent forty years preaching short, plain sermons to farmers and tradesmen who could not follow a rhetorician. Some two hundred and fifty survive, and their deliberate simplicity is itself a doctrine: the Word is for the people. His lasting service to the church, however, was the Second Council of Orange in 529, over which he presided and whose canons he largely framed. Orange put down the Semi-Pelagianism of Faustus of Riez and settled, for the Western church, that grace precedes the first motion of the will. Its canons say what Joh 15:16 says — “Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you” — and what Rom 9:16 says, “it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.” Eph 2:5 is the whole of it: God “quickened us together with Christ” while we were dead. The Reformers appealed to Orange constantly, and rightly: it is the clearest patristic statement of sovereign grace that an official council ever produced, and the bishop of Arles is the reason it exists.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grace, in theology, as the free unmerited love and favour of God, and prevenient grace as that which goes before.
webster_full: GRACE, n. Favour; good will; kindness.
2. Appropriately, the free unmerited love and favour of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
4. The application of Christ's righteousness to the sinner.
scriptures: Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain: that whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you.
Eph 2:5
Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;)
Php 2:13
For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.
Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
corruption_summary: Orange is the council the church forgot, and the forgetting is how Semi-Pelagianism became the ordinary religion of Christendom again within two centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: Orange settled the question and the settlement did not hold. Within two hundred years the practical teaching of the Western church had drifted back to a grace that assists a will already moving, and by the later Middle Ages the scheme Orange condemned was the common doctrine of the schools. The Reformation's appeal to Orange was therefore not an innovation but a demand that the church keep its own canons. The same drift runs in every age, because the doctrine that a man contributes the first step is the most natural thing a fallen heart can believe. Php 2:13 forecloses it: “it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure” — the willing included.

The second corruption is the modern treatment of Caesarius as a pastoral figure whose council was a regional administrative act of little weight. That judgment is convenient for anyone who wishes the fathers to be uniformly synergistic. Orange is a genuine conciliar witness, confirmed by Boniface II, and it teaches prevenient and effectual grace. The recovery is to read it: a council of Gallic bishops, a century after Augustine, confessing that the beginning of faith is itself the gift of God.
roots_summary: Greek eklegomai (G1586), to choose out; suzoopoieo (G4806), to quicken together; energeo (G1754), to work effectually.
roots_lines: Greek eklegomai (G1586) — to choose out, to elect; John 15:16.
Greek suzoopoieo (G4806) — to make alive together with; Ephesians 2:5.
Greek energeo (G1754) — to work in, to be operative; Philippians 2:13.
Greek eleeo (G1653) — to shew mercy; Romans 9:16.
Greek thelo (G2309) — to will, to be willing; Romans 9:16, Philippians 2:13.
usage: “Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you” (Joh 15:16) — the order Orange restored.
“it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure” (Php 2:13) — the willing itself a gift.
“it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16) — the canon in one verse.

pos: n. (the Venerable Bede, c. 673–735, monk of Jarrow, author of the Ecclesiastical History of the English People and the first great scholar of the English church)
etymology: Old English Bæda, of uncertain sense; the epithet Venerabilis was attached within a century of his death.
biblical_def: Bede entered the monastery at Wearmouth as a boy of seven and remained in that double house at Jarrow until he died, by his own account spending his life in learning, teaching and writing. He is the father of English history: the Ecclesiastical History is the only coherent account of the conversion of the Anglo-Saxons, and it is written with a care for sources — named informants, quoted letters, admitted uncertainty — that no contemporary matched. He wrote far more commentary than history, and reckoned the commentaries his real work. He also fixed the computus by which Easter was calculated and popularized dating from the incarnation, so that Psa 90:12, “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom,” has a literal application to him. The scene of his death, told by his pupil Cuthbert, is the measure of the man: he was dictating a translation of John's Gospel into English and finished the last sentence before he died. He is the Act 17:11 Berean in a Northumbrian cell, one who “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines venerable as worthy of veneration or reverence; deserving of honor and respect; rendered sacred by religious associations, or being consecrated to God.
webster_full: VEN'ERABLE, a. Worthy of veneration or reverence; deserving of honor and respect; as a venerable magistrate.
2. Rendered sacred by religious associations, or being consecrated to God and to his worship.
The hoary head is venerable, when found in the way of righteousness.
scriptures: Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
corruption_summary: Bede is read now as a source to be mined and a chronicler to be corrected, and almost never as what he was, an expositor of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern use of Bede is almost entirely historical: his History is quarried for the Anglo-Saxon centuries and his dozens of commentaries sit unread. Bede would have thought the proportion absurd. He wrote history as a branch of edification, saying plainly in his preface that the reader should imitate the good he finds and shun the evil, and he reckoned his exposition of Genesis, Luke and the Acts the weightier labour. To take the chronicle and leave the commentary is to take a man's notes and discard his argument, and it quietly teaches that the useful part of a Christian scholar is whatever a secular reader can use.

The second corruption is the opposite error of the shrine. Bede's bones were stolen for Durham and he was made a saint to be invoked, which is precisely the honour he would have refused; his own account of Cuthbert is already heavy with the relic-piety that Scripture forbids. The lawful honour is the one Bede himself practised toward the fathers: read what he wrote, test it by the Word, and do as he did — pray Psa 119:18, “Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law,” and then work at the text until the day you die.
roots_summary: Greek anakrino (G350), to examine, to sift; theopneustos (G2315), God-breathed; Hebrew galah (H1540), to uncover.
roots_lines: Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to sift judicially; Acts 17:11.
Greek theopneustos (G2315) — God-breathed, inspired; 2 Timothy 3:16.
Hebrew galah (H1540) — to uncover, to open; Psalm 119:18.
Hebrew manah (H4487) — to number, to appoint; Psalm 90:12.
Hebrew pala (H6381) — wondrous, surpassing; Psalm 119:18.

“searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) — his method in a cell.
“So teach us to number our days” (Psa 90:12) — the computist's text.

pos: n. (Gregory of Tours, 538–594, bishop of Tours and author of the History of the Franks, the chief source for Merovingian Gaul)
etymology: Greek Gregorios, watchful, from gregoreo, to be awake; Tours is the Roman Caesarodunum on the Loire.
biblical_def: Gregory of Tours came of a Gallo-Roman senatorial family that had given bishops to Gaul for generations, and he held the see of Tours for twenty-one years in the thick of Merovingian politics. His ten books of Histories are the indispensable record of the Frankish kingdoms, and their value lies in their unsparing candour: Gregory tells of kings who murdered their brothers, queens who strangled rivals, and bishops who bought their sees, and he tells it of his own patrons. He writes as a man who believes Pro 14:34, that “Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people,” and who sees the proof in every chapter. Jer 17:9 is his working anthropology — “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked” — and he does not except the baptized. He also holds Rom 13:1 with a plain conscience, that “the powers that be are ordained of God,” while rebuking the powers to their faces. His Latin is rough and he apologizes for it; his theology is thin and his appetite for miracles at the tombs of saints is large. But as a witness to what men are, he is nearly without equal in his century.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chronicle as a historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time; and annals as a relation of events in chronological order.
webster_full: CHRON'ICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
AN'NALS, n. A species of history digested in order of time, or a relation of events in chronological order, each event being recorded under the year in which it happened.
scriptures: Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.
Jer 17:9
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
Ecc 1:9
The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
corruption_summary: Gregory's Gaul is read either as proof that Christendom was a sham or as a picturesque dark age, and both readings miss the doctrine his own pages teach.
corruption_paragraphs: A favourite modern use of the History of the Franks is to show that the conversion of Europe changed nothing, since Clovis's Christian descendants behaved like heathen. Gregory would answer that this is exactly what Scripture predicts of unregenerate men who have been baptized, and that his book is an extended commentary on Jer 17:9. A nation may receive the name of Christ by its king's decision and remain full of men whose hearts are unchanged; that is the argument against sacral mass conversion, not against the gospel. The corruption lies in treating national Christianization as if it were regeneration, an error the Merovingians made and the critics now assume on their behalf.

The second corruption is the one Gregory himself carried: his pages are thick with cures at tombs and the power of relics, and his Glory of the Martyrs is a catalogue of them. This is the shrine-piety the Reformation swept away, and no amount of historical sympathy makes it harmless, for it puts the help of the living God at a dead man's grave. The recovery is to take his candour and refuse his superstition: “there is no new thing under the sun” (Ecc 1:9) covers the sins of kings and the credulity of bishops alike.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsedaqah (H6666), righteousness; aqob (H6121), deceitful, crooked; Greek exousia (G1849), authority.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsedaqah (H6666) — righteousness; Proverbs 14:34.
Hebrew aqob (H6121) — deceitful, crooked; Jeremiah 17:9.
Hebrew anash (H605) — desperately sick, incurable; Jeremiah 17:9.
Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, the higher powers; Romans 13:1.
Greek tasso (G5021) — to appoint, to ordain; Romans 13:1.

“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked” (Jer 17:9) — his anthropology, proved page by page.
“the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1) — held while rebuking them.

pos: n. (Alcuin of York, c. 735–804, English scholar, master of Charlemagne's palace school and abbot of Tours, the chief architect of the Carolingian revival of learning)
etymology: Old English Ealhwine, temple-friend; Latinized Alcuinus, and he also signed himself Albinus.
biblical_def: Alcuin was trained in the cathedral school at York, the best library in the West, and was recruited by Charlemagne in 781 to teach at the palace. What followed was the Carolingian renaissance: schools attached to cathedrals and monasteries, a reformed hand that is the ancestor of our printed letter-forms, and a corrected text of the Vulgate prepared under his direction, since the copies then circulating were full of error. He wrote on grammar, dialectic and orthodoxy, and answered the Adoptionism of Felix of Urgel, who taught that Christ was Son of God by adoption in His humanity. His finest hour was a letter to Charlemagne about the Saxons, whom the emperor was baptizing at the point of the sword and taxing for tithes: Alcuin argued that faith is of the will and cannot be forced, that a man must be taught before he is washed, and that Rom 10:17 governs the order — “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” Mat 28:19 puts teaching with baptizing, and Alcuin saw what his master did not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to catechise as to instruct by asking questions, receiving answers, and offering explanations and corrections, particularly in the principles of religion.
webster_full: CAT'ECHISE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions, receiving answers, and offering explanations and corrections.
2. To question; to interrogate; to examine or try by questions.
To instruct in the principles of the Christian religion, by means of questions and answers.
scriptures: So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
corruption_summary: Alcuin told an emperor that a forced baptism is no baptism, and Christendom spent the next eight centuries proving he was right.
corruption_paragraphs: Charlemagne's Saxon policy — conversion by conquest, baptism on pain of death, tithes exacted from the newly washed — is the purest form of the sacral error, and Alcuin opposed it on the ground that belief cannot be compelled. He was not a Baptist and did not draw the conclusion the 1689 Confession draws, but his argument runs that way: if faith comes by hearing, then the hearing must come first, and a sacrament given to an unbeliever at swordpoint signifies nothing. Mat 28:19 commands the church to “teach all nations, baptizing them” — the participle follows the teaching, and reversing them produced a Europe full of baptized pagans.

The second corruption is the modern reduction of the Carolingian revival to a cultural programme, as though Alcuin cared chiefly for script and syntax. He corrected the Vulgate because men were reading a faulty Bible, taught grammar so that they could read it, and catechized because Deu 6:7 commands that the words be taught diligently to children. Learning in his hands is instrumental to the Word. The recovery is to keep that order and to refuse the two errors Alcuin faced: a church that will not teach, and a magistrate who thinks he can command faith.
roots_summary: Greek akoe (G189), hearing, the thing heard; matheteuo (G3100), to make disciples, to teach; orthotomeo (G3718), to divide rightly.
roots_lines: Greek akoe (G189) — hearing, the report heard; Romans 10:17.
Greek matheteuo (G3100) — to make a disciple, to teach; Matthew 28:19.
Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, to divide rightly; 2 Timothy 2:15.
Hebrew shanan (H8150) — to sharpen, hence to teach diligently; Deuteronomy 6:7.

“teach all nations, baptizing them” (Mat 28:19) — the order Charlemagne reversed.
“thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children” (Deu 6:7) — why he built schools.

pos: n. (Boniface of Mainz, c. 675–754, born Wynfrith in Wessex, missionary archbishop among the Germans and martyr in Frisia; called the apostle of Germany)
etymology: Latin Bonifatius, well-doer, from bonum facere — a name given him at Rome; his English name was Wynfrith, friend of peace.
biblical_def: Boniface of Mainz left a comfortable English monastery in middle life to preach among the heathen Germans, and laboured at it for thirty-five years. The famous act of his career was at Geismar, where he took an axe to the oak sacred to Thunor in the sight of the people who expected the god to strike him down. Nothing happened, and he built a chapel from the timber. It is Gideon's deed in Jdg 6:25, throwing down the altar of Baal and cutting down the grove beside it, and the command of Deu 7:5 — “ye shall destroy their altars, and break down their images, and cut down their groves.” He planted churches and monasteries across Hesse, Thuringia and Bavaria, reformed the corrupt Frankish clergy in a series of synods, and at near eighty went back to the unconverted Frisians, where he was killed with some fifty companions while waiting to confirm new converts. He had told his people not to fight. Act 20:24 is his epitaph: “neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy.” 1Th 1:9 is the fruit he sought, that men “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a grove, in Scripture use, as a place where idolatrous rites were performed, often rendering the Hebrew for a wooden image or an Asherah.
webster_full: GROVE, n. A cluster of trees of considerable extent.
2. A wood of small extent.
In Scripture, groves are mentioned as places of idolatrous worship, and the word often denotes the idol or wooden image itself.
scriptures: Deu 7:5
But thus shall ye deal with them; ye shall destroy their altars, and break down their images, and cut down their groves, and burn their graven images with fire.
Jdg 6:25

And it came to pass the same night, that the LORD said unto him, Take thy father's young bullock, even the second bullock of seven years old, and throw down the altar of Baal that thy father hath, and cut down the grove that is by it:
For they themselves shew of us what manner of entering in we had unto you, and how ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God;

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
corruption_summary: Boniface is the missionary who felled the idol and then bound the churches he planted to the Roman see, and both halves of that work went to Germany together.
corruption_paragraphs: Boniface took his commission from Rome, swore obedience to the pope, and made the German church papal in a way the older Celtic and Frankish missions had not been. The bishop of Rome gained from him an authority north of the Alps that would take eight centuries and a German monk to break, and when Luther appealed against that authority he was contending with an arrangement Boniface had built. Honour the axe at Geismar and name the other thing plainly: the gospel does not travel with a see attached, and the apostle's own charge in Act 20:24 is to “testify the gospel of the grace of God,” not to extend a jurisdiction.

The second corruption is the sentimental modern reading that makes Geismar a parable of cultural insensitivity — the European felling the sacred tree of an indigenous people. Scripture does not permit the framing. Deu 7:5 commands the destruction of the groves because the groves are where men damn themselves, and the kindest act available to Boniface was to prove in public that the god could not defend his own oak. The recovery is to keep the courage and drop the jurisdiction: preach until men turn “from idols to serve the living and true God” (1Th 1:9), and plant churches that answer to Christ.

roots_lines: Hebrew asherah (H842) — a grove, a wooden image; Deuteronomy 7:5, Judges 6:25.

“cut down the grove that is by it” (Jdg 6:25) — Gideon's precedent.
“neither count I my life dear unto myself” (Act 20:24) — his end in Frisia.

pos: n. (Ansgar, 801–865, monk of Corbie, archbishop of Hamburg and papal legate to the North, called the apostle of the North for his missions to Denmark and Sweden)
etymology: Old Norse and Germanic Ansgar, god-spear, from ans, a god, and gar, a spear; also Anskar and Oscar.
biblical_def: Ansgar was a monk of Corbie sent in 826 with the exiled Danish king Harald, and he spent the next forty years attempting the conversion of Scandinavia. The record is one of almost unbroken reverse. He built a church and a school at Hedeby and saw them closed; he preached in Sweden at Birka and won a few; his cathedral at Hamburg was burned by a Viking fleet in 845 and his whole province was lost; he was reduced to Bremen and began again. He bought slave boys to train as preachers to their own people. At his death there was scarcely a Christian nation in the North to show for it, and Scandinavia was not Christianized for another century and a half. He is the standing illustration of 1Co 3:6 — “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” — and of Psa 126:6, “He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing.” Gal 6:9 was his daily text: “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.” The season came long after his grave was closed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a missionary as one sent to propagate religion; and to plant, in its figurative sense, as to set or introduce for the first time.
webster_full: MISS'IONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion.
PLANT, v.t. To set in the ground for growth.
4. To introduce and establish; as, to plant Christianity among the heathen.
scriptures: I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
Isa 49:6

And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth.
Gal 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
corruption_summary: A mission is judged now by the increase it can report, and by that standard Ansgar failed for forty years — which is the standard Scripture does not use.
corruption_paragraphs: The metrics culture of modern missions would have closed Ansgar's field in his first decade. He had burned churches, scattered converts and nothing to put in a report. But 1Co 3:6 divides the labour from the result and assigns the increase to God alone, which means faithfulness is the only thing a man can be asked for. The error is not in counting — Acts counts — but in making the count the measure of obedience, so that a field God has appointed to be sown for a century without harvest looks like disobedience and is abandoned.

The second corruption is the triumphalist retelling that quietly supplies him a success. Popular accounts credit Ansgar with the conversion of Scandinavia, which is simply untrue and robs his life of its real lesson. The honest account is better: he sowed, he saw almost nothing, he did not quit, and the harvest came in God's season to other men's hands. That is the pattern of Psa 126:6, and it is also the comfort of Isa 49:6, where the servant is given “for a light to the Gentiles” — a promise fulfilled on God's calendar, not the missionary's.
roots_summary: Greek phuteuo (G5452), to plant; auxano (G837), to cause to grow; ekkakeo (G1573), to grow weary.
roots_lines: Greek phuteuo (G5452) — to plant; 1 Corinthians 3:6.
Greek auxano (G837) — to make to grow, to give increase; 1 Corinthians 3:6.
Greek ekkakeo (G1573) — to lose heart, to be weary; Galatians 6:9.
Hebrew zera (H2233) — seed; Psalm 126:6.
Hebrew or (H216) — light; Isaiah 49:6.
usage: “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6) — the division of labour he lived under.
“He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed” (Psa 126:6) — forty years of it.
“let us not be weary in well doing” (Gal 6:9) — his text against the evidence.

pos: n. (Odo of Cluny, c. 878–942, second abbot of Cluny, the chief promoter of the Cluniac reform of monastic discipline and of monastic liberty from lay control)
etymology: Germanic Odo, from od, wealth or patrimony; Cluny is in Burgundy, founded 910 by William the Pious of Aquitaine.
biblical_def: Odo of Cluny took charge of a house whose founding charter had done something unusual: it placed the abbey under the pope and expressly out of the reach of the local lord, so that no count could sell its offices or install his son as abbot. Odo made that liberty into a movement. Invited to reform house after house in France and Italy, he restored the Benedictine rule where it had lapsed, lengthened the hours of worship, insisted on genuine poverty, and left Cluny the head of a network that would reckon hundreds of dependent monasteries. His own writings are severe, and his Collations read like 2Ch 29:5 applied to the cloister: “sanctify now yourselves, and sanctify the house of the LORD God of your fathers, and carry forth the filthiness out of the holy place.” He saw plainly what Luk 16:13 says, that no servant can serve two masters, and that a monastery owned by a nobleman serves the nobleman. The reform he began produced, within a century and a half, the men who undertook to reform the papacy itself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to reform as to change from worse to better; to amend; to correct; to restore to a former good state.
webster_full: REFORM', v.t. To change from worse to better; to amend; to correct; to restore to a former good state, or to bring from a bad to a good state.
2. To change from bad to good; to remove that which is bad or corrupt.
REFORM', v.i. To abandon that which is evil or corrupt, and return to a good state.
scriptures: And said unto them, Hear me, ye Levites, sanctify now yourselves, and sanctify the house of the LORD God of your fathers, and carry forth the filthiness out of the holy place.
Because it is written, Be ye holy; for I am holy.
Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord:
No servant can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
corruption_summary: Cluny proves that a reform of discipline without a reform of doctrine produces a cleaner version of the same error, and in time a richer one.
corruption_paragraphs: The Cluniac reform was a real work: it broke lay ownership of the monasteries, put down simony in the houses it touched, and restored a discipline that had collapsed. But it reformed practice and left doctrine where it found it. Cluny's immense round of intercessory offices for the dead, its traffic in masses, and the wealth that poured in from men buying prayers were not corrected but enlarged, until the abbey that began in poverty was among the richest institutions in Europe. The lesson is the one the sixteenth century had to learn: discipline without the gospel yields a disciplined works-religion.

Scripture sets the order the other way. “Be ye holy; for I am holy” (1Pe 1:16) is a command grounded in what God is and, in the New Testament, addressed to a people already redeemed; holiness follows justification and does not purchase it. The recovery is to want everything Odo wanted — a church not owned by the powerful, offices not for sale, ministers who are not hirelings — and to seek it on the foundation he lacked, since a house swept clean and furnished with merit is not yet a Christian house.

roots_lines: Hebrew qadash (H6942) — to sanctify, to consecrate; 2 Chronicles 29:5.
Hebrew niddah (H5079) — filthiness, that which is put away; 2 Chronicles 29:5.
Greek hagios (G40) — holy, set apart; 1 Peter 1:16.
Greek hagiasmos (G38) — holiness, sanctification; Hebrews 12:14.
Greek douleuo (G1398) — to serve as a bondman; Luke 16:13.
usage: “carry forth the filthiness out of the holy place” (2Ch 29:5) — the Cluniac programme in a clause.
“Be ye holy; for I am holy” (1Pe 1:16) — the ground he rightly appealed to.
“No servant can serve two masters” (Luk 16:13) — against the abbey owned by a count.

pos: n. (Peter Damian, 1007–1072, hermit of Fonte Avellana, cardinal-bishop of Ostia, fierce reformer of clerical morals and ally of Hildebrand)
etymology: Latin Petrus Damianus; the surname is probably from a brother named Damianus who raised him, not a place.
biblical_def: Peter Damian was born poor at Ravenna, became a hermit in the Apennines, and was dragged out of his cell by successive popes to do the work of the eleventh-century reform. He was made cardinal-bishop of Ostia against his will and used the office to attack the two great scandals of the clergy: the purchase of church office and the open concubinage of priests. His Liber Gomorrhianus lays the vices of the clergy before Pope Leo IX in language no modern churchman would print, on the principle of 1Ti 3:2 that “A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife,” and of Tit 1:7, “not given to filthy lucre.” He was a genuine ascetic who scourged himself, slept little, ate less, and commended the discipline to others as a way of satisfying for sin. He also coined the formula that philosophy should be the handmaid of theology. His courage was real and his doctrine of the body was not: Col 2:23 names the error of “neglecting of the body” that has “a shew of wisdom in will worship,” and 1Ti 4:8 says plainly that “bodily exercise profiteth little.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines asceticism as the state or practice of an ascetic; and an ascetic as one who retires from the customary business of life, and devotes himself to the duties of piety and devotion; a hermit.
webster_full: ASCET'IC, n. One who retires from the customary business of life, and devotes himself to the duties of piety and devotion; a hermit; a recluse.
ASCET'IC, a. Unduly rigid in devotions and mortifications.
MORTIFICA'TION, n. The act of subduing the passions and appetites by penance, abstinence, or painful severities inflicted on the body.
scriptures: A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
Tit 1:7
For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre;
Col 2:23
Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
corruption_summary: Peter Damian attacked real corruption with real courage and prescribed a false remedy, so that the cure he urged on the church was itself a doctrine needing reform.
corruption_paragraphs: The abuses Damian denounced were genuine, and Scripture arms him: a bishop must be blameless, and a clergy that buys its offices and keeps concubines has forfeited the office. But the remedy he pressed was penance, self-scourging and the merit of a mortified body, and that remedy is the disease in another form. Col 2:23 judges it exactly — a shew of wisdom in will worship and the neglecting of the body, “not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.” Sin is not paid for by a whip. The eleventh-century reform cleaned the clergy's conduct while deepening its works-religion, which is why the real reformation had to wait for the recovery of justification.

The second error is the enforced celibacy that Damian did more than almost any man to impose. Scripture requires a bishop to be “the husband of one wife” (1Ti 3:2), which assumes marriage rather than forbidding it, and 1Ti 4:1-3 names the forbidding of marriage as a doctrine of devils. Rome diagnosed clerical immorality and prescribed the prohibition that had helped produce it. The recovery is the plain qualification list of the Pastorals: married elders of proven character, plural in each congregation, holding no office for sale and needing no scourge.
roots_summary: Greek anepileptos (G423), blameless; aischrokerdes (G146), greedy of filthy lucre; ethelothreskeia (G1479), will worship.
roots_lines: Greek anepileptos (G423) — not open to censure, blameless; 1 Timothy 3:2.
Greek aischrokerdes (G146) — greedy of base gain; Titus 1:7.
Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479) — self-chosen worship, will worship; Colossians 2:23.

usage: “A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife” (1Ti 3:2) — the standard he held against the clergy.
“not given to filthy lucre” (Tit 1:7) — his charge against simony.
“For bodily exercise profiteth little” (1Ti 4:8) — the verse his remedy ignored.
